title: Divided daily doses: mg/kg/day split into single doses
blurb: Turn a mg/kg/day prescription into the single dose and volume to give, dividing by the right number of doses.
question: A child weighing 20 kg is prescribed a medicine at 60 mg/kg/day given 6-hourly. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose?

teach.h: Daily dose, then share it out
teach.body: Formal rule: single dose = (dose per kg per day × weight in kg) ÷ number of doses per day. Plain English: "mg/kg/day" tells you the whole day's amount for this child; the frequency tells you how many equal parts to split it into. Then measure one part. This pattern is standard in children's prescribing and in the NMC numeracy blueprint.

teach.h: Worked example: Noah on a children's ward
teach.body: Noah, 6, weighs 20 kg and is prescribed 60 mg/kg/day 6-hourly. The suspension is 250 mg/5 mL. Daily total = 60 × 20 = 1200 mg. 6-hourly = 4 doses, so one dose = 1200 ÷ 4 = 300 mg. Volume = 300 ÷ 250 × 5 = 6 mL. Sense-check: 4 × 6 mL = 24 mL a day, which holds 1200 mg ✓.

teach.caption: The "/day" changes the answer threefold or fourfold. Read it carefully.

teach.text: Giving the whole daily dose as one dose: forgetting to divide a mg/kg/day figure by the number of doses gives three or four times the intended single dose. A second trap is dividing by the hour interval (6-hourly ÷ 6) instead of the number of doses (÷ 4).

teach.h: Which number do I divide by?

teach.body: Daily totals for babies often produce awkward single doses (for example 32 mg from 120 mg/5 mL = 1.333… mL). Keep the full calculator value and round only the final volume to the instruction, usually two decimal places for children.

items: Daily total = mg/kg/day × weight in kg.
Single dose = daily total ÷ number of doses per day.
Classic error: giving the daily total as a single dose.
Then volume = single dose ÷ label strength × stock volume.

summary: You can now split a mg/kg/day prescription into equal single doses using the right number of doses per day, and turn each dose into a volume. You can also check that the single doses add back up to the daily total.

A.q: A child weighing 15 kg is prescribed a medicine at 30 mg/kg/day in three divided doses. What is each single dose?
A.why: Daily total = 30 × 15 = 450 mg. Single dose = 450 ÷ 3 = 150 mg.

whyNot.0: This is the daily total, not a single dose.
whyNot.2: Divided per-kg figure by doses but forgot the weight.
whyNot.3: Divided into two doses, not three.

A.q: A child weighing 22 kg is prescribed a medicine at 40 mg/kg/day given 6-hourly. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
A.why: Daily = 40 × 22 = 880 mg. 6-hourly = 4 doses: 880 ÷ 4 = 220 mg. Volume = 220 ÷ 250 × 5 = 4.4 mL.

whyNot.0: This is the whole day's volume, not one dose.
whyNot.1: Divided by 6 (the interval) instead of 4 doses.
whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.

A.q: A baby weighing 8 kg is prescribed a medicine at 40 mg/kg/day in two divided doses. What is each single dose?
A.why: Daily total = 40 × 8 = 320 mg. Single dose = 320 ÷ 2 = 160 mg.

whyNot.2: Divided into four doses, not two.
whyNot.3: Divided by the weight instead of multiplying.

B.q: A child weighing 13 kg is prescribed a medicine at 45 mg/kg/day in three divided doses. The oral suspension is labelled 125 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
B.why: Daily = 45 × 13 = 585 mg. Single dose = 585 ÷ 3 = 195 mg. Volume = 195 ÷ 125 × 5 = 7.8 mL.

whyNot.0: This is the daily volume, not one dose.
whyNot.1: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Divided into two doses, not three.

B.q: A child weighing 9.5 kg is prescribed a medicine at 20 mg/kg/day given 12-hourly. The oral suspension is labelled 100 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
B.why: Daily = 20 × 9.5 = 190 mg. 12-hourly = 2 doses: 95 mg. Volume = 95 ÷ 100 × 5 = 4.75 mL.

whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Divided by 12 (the interval) instead of 2 doses.

B.q: A child weighing 24 kg is prescribed a medicine at 25 mg/kg/day given 8-hourly. What is each single dose?

whyNot.1: Divided by 8 (the interval) instead of 3 doses.
whyNot.2: Divided into four doses instead of three.

C.q: A child weighing 17 kg is prescribed a medicine at 50 mg/kg/day in four divided doses. The oral suspension is labelled 250 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.

whyNot.2: Rounded to one decimal place; the stem asks for two.
whyNot.3: Divided into three doses instead of four.

C.q: A baby weighing 6400 g is prescribed a medicine at 15 mg/kg/day in three divided doses. The oral suspension is labelled 120 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to two decimal places.
C.why: Weight = 6.4 kg. Daily = 15 × 6.4 = 96 mg. Single dose = 96 ÷ 3 = 32 mg. Volume = 32 ÷ 120 × 5 = 1.333…, which is 1.33 mL.

whyNot.0: Left the weight in grams: 1000 times too much.
whyNot.1: This is the daily volume, not one dose.
whyNot.3: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.

C.q: A child weighing 11 kg is prescribed a medicine at 80 mg/kg/day in two divided doses. The oral suspension is labelled 400 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit and write your answer to one decimal place.
C.why: Daily = 80 × 11 = 880 mg. Single dose = 880 ÷ 2 = 440 mg. Volume = 440 ÷ 400 × 5 = 5.5 mL.

whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Divided into three doses instead of two.

reteach.title: The "/day" means divide
reteach.question: A child needs 600 mg a day in three divided doses. How much is one dose?

blocks.body: Three divided doses means three equal parts of the daily total: 600 ÷ 3 = 200 mg each. Check: 3 × 200 = 600 ✓.

blocks.text: Giving 600 mg at each dose would give 1800 mg in a day: three times the prescription.

explain.body: Daily total = mg/kg/day × weight. Do not divide yet.

test.q: A child weighing 18 kg is prescribed a medicine at 40 mg/kg/day. What is the total daily dose?

whyNot.0: This divides the 720 mg by three doses; the question asks for the total daily dose, not a single dose.
whyNot.1: Divided weight by the per-kg dose.
whyNot.2: Weight taken as 180 kg, a tenfold slip.

test.q: A child's total daily dose is 900 mg in three divided doses. What is each single dose?
A child's total daily dose is 1000 mg given 6-hourly. What is each single dose?

whyNot.0: Divided by the interval (6) instead of 4 doses.

explain.body: Use the single dose as WANT: volume = single dose ÷ label mg × label volume.

test.q: A child weighing 14 kg is prescribed a medicine at 25 mg/kg/day in two divided doses. The oral suspension is labelled 125 mg/5 mL. What volume should be given for each dose? Please use the correct unit.
test.why: Daily = 25 × 14 = 350 mg. Single dose = 175 mg. Volume = 175 ÷ 125 × 5 = 7 mL.

whyNot.2: Forgot to multiply by the 5 mL stock volume.
whyNot.3: Divided into three doses instead of two.
